newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Luxembourg amending law to target drug lords.
newsitem.headline: Luxembourg amending law to target drug lords.

text.p: Tiny Luxembourg, with the highest proportion of hard drug addicts in the European Union, plans to relax the law for cannabis users and focus on tracking down big-time drug traffickers.
The proposals, laid out in a new draft law, also place heavy emphasis on preventing drug abuse and extending existing projects which help those already addicted.
Luxembourg Justice Minister Marc Fischbach is careful to stress, however, that the move is not about liberalisation.

"The motivation is...to put more emphasis on prevention than on repression. The addict must be thought of as someone who is sick and in need of help, not a prison sentence," he told Reuters on Friday.

"That doesn't mean we are going to decriminalise drug use, and trafficking. We will keep sanctions for both, but will clearly differentiate between soft or "low" risk drugs, and "high" risk drugs," he added.

Currently, Luxembourg police clamp down on both hard and soft drugs alike, as the law does not distinguish between them. On paper at least, ongoing drugs-related projects to help users, such as syringe exchanges, are illegal.

Fischbach said that under the new law, there would no longer be a prison sentence for users of soft drugs, namely cannabis and its derivatives, though the courts could still impose a fine of up to 100,000 Luxembourg francs ($2,620).
Currently all drug users, in theory at least, risk a maximum sentence of three years.

"For users of high-risk drugs we will maintain a prison sentence," he added. "This is not a way to dissuade them...but it could be that in a case of extreme distress, the judge has no choice but to pass a custodial sentence in order to force the user to follow treatment in prison."
Luxembourg, an affluent country, says it has 2,000 hard drug users, making up 0.5 percent of the population.
This compares to 0.28 percent in neighbouring -- and much larger -- France, and from between 0.16 to 0.2 percent in the Netherlands, which is renowned for its liberal drug policy.
Fischbach said the new law also aimed to make the fight against trafficking more effective.
Traffickers will still face sentences of up to five years.

But those who reveal crucial information on others which helps police get to those higher up in the trafficking chain could see their potential sentences lifted or reduced, provided they give give the information voluntarily before legal proceedings are started against them.
The law also gives a legal basis to ongoing projects such as a methadone substitution programme, which the minister said had helped reduce the number of drug overdoses among addicts.

By 1996, there were 128 people using the methadone substitution programme, compared to just 51 two years before, and the number of fatal overdoses in Luxembourg has fallen steadily however, from 29 cases in 1994 to just 16 in 1996.

The new law provides for special meeting places to be set up where addicts can use drugs hygienically, and also for a strictly limited drug distribution programme, reserved for addicts considered by appointed doctors as being at risk of overdose.
The draft will be sent to parliament in August and is expected to be voted through by the end of this year or early next year, Fischbach said. ($ = 38.10 Luxembourg Francs)
